The All Progressives Congress has defended President Bola Tinubu’s handling of insecurity, claiming that the country has recorded a reduction in attacks and fatalities since he assumed office in 2023. The party’s National Publicity Secretary, Felix Morka, made the assertion on Wednesday during an appearance on Channels Television’s The Morning Brief, where he highlighted what he described as improvements in the military’s capacity and the welfare of its personnel. Morka attributed the progress to measures introduced by the administration, including improved remuneration for soldiers, an increase in military personnel and better working conditions. He stated, “Over the last year, we have witnessed a consistent decline, both in terms of incidents of insecurity, in terms of you know, fatalities.” He also pointed to the creation of additional army divisions and improved accommodation for military personnel as evidence of the government’s efforts to strengthen the armed forces. “You know, I mean, is it the creation of, you know, more divisions of the army? Is it the better motivation of our soldiers who are fighting and putting their lives, you know, in a line of fire every day for our safety? Is it, you know, building, you know, safer accommodation for our soldiers?” he added. Make PUNCH part of your everyday experience. He said even countries with sophisticated security systems had been unable to eliminate threats completely, adding that the challenge could not be resolved overnight. He noted, “You know, insecurity is not something that is extinguished overnight, Nigeria, not by the most sophisticated countries on earth, not by the United States, not by Israel. “Some of the, you know, most effective, you know, states, national security-conscious states, have not managed to eliminate insecurity altogether. Now, I’m not saying that we’re not challenged.” Obi denies seeking US lawmakers’ backing for 2027 race PHOTOS: Army commandant decorates three senior officers in Lagos Army intercepts ammunition supplier, recovers 300 bullets in Kogi Morka further claimed that government security interventions had led to the surrender of more terrorists and bandits to the military. He maintained that the administration had made considerable gains in tackling insecurity and urged media organisations to report the situation in a balanced manner, insisting that the government’s efforts and results should be recognised. His comments followed criticism by the presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress, Peter Obi, who had raised concerns about the security situation in the country. In a statement published in August, Obi warned against allowing Nigeria to become a ‘killing field’, citing attacks and abductions in parts of the North-Central region. He expressed concern that communities were being attacked and residents displaced despite the country not being officially at war. “Nigeria is not officially at war, yet citizens are being attacked in their villages, abducted after prayers, driven from their homes and stripped of their farms,” he said. Nigeria continues to face multiple security threats, including insurgency by extremist groups, banditry, kidnappings and communal violence. The Global Centre for the Responsibility to Protect, in a November 16 assessment, said attacks by armed bandit groups and Boko Haram and Islamic State West Africa Province militants continued to put civilians at risk. In his August statement, Obi called on governments at all levels to strengthen intelligence gathering, improve rapid-response capabilities, protect vulnerable communities and intensify efforts to rescue abducted Nigerians.
